Comprehensive adversarial SECURITY AUDIT of the ENTIRE Nxeon shared-hosting attack surface — not just recent changes. Shared hosting is LIVE in production (ENABLE_SHARED_HOSTING=1, a real customer account on node hosting-1) and about to get paid ad traffic. Threat model: a MALICIOUS PAYING TENANT ($3.29 buys a PHP + cron + SFTP foothold) trying to (a) escape the jail to the host, (b) reach another tenant's files/DB/mail, or (c) DoS the box. Read-only — do NOT modify files, do NOT SSH or run anything against any node. Produce ONE prioritized findings report.

Read the whole surface (branch feature/shared-hosting-p0 in worktree /opt/nxeon-wt-host is the latest; also compare to what's live if useful):
- worker/hosting.ts — the FULL provisioner: applyIsolation (jailed user creation, FPM pool with open_basedir/disable_functions, disk quota, vhost), all task handlers (WordPress/app installs, backups/restore, PHP switch, DB create, subdomain/addon/cron, the new health/self-heal sweep + self-signed cert generation), the SSH exec helpers.
- lib/hosting.ts — every pure validator + the fpmPoolConfig generator (is open_basedir tight? disable_functions complete — pcntl_exec, proc_open, popen, shell_exec, system, passthru, ffi, dl, putenv, mail? is /tmp shared or per-user? can a tenant read /etc/nginx, other /home dirs, the platform's secrets?).
- lib/hosting-fs.ts — the file manager jail (OS chroot vs lexical).
- lib/actions-hosting.ts — authz/IDOR/impersonation/TOCTOU on every action.
- scripts/onboard-hosting-node.sh — the box hardening (fail2ban, ModSecurity, ClamAV, quota, sshd chroot, MariaDB) — what's actually enforced vs staged.
- prisma/schema.prisma hosting models.

Specifically probe: PHP jail escapes (disable_functions bypasses, open_basedir bypasses via symlink/proc, LD_PRELOAD, writable cron/system dirs); cross-tenant reads (world-readable homes, shared tmp, MySQL grants, socket perms); privilege escalation (SUID, sudo, writable service files, the FPM pool running as the right user, the self-signed cert openssl command); resource exhaustion (no CPU/mem/pids/inode caps = one tenant DoSes all — CONFIRM whether any exist); the WordPress/app install + backup/restore paths for injection or cross-tenant writes; the new self-heal sweep reinstalling vhosts.

For each finding: severity (CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW), file:line, concrete exploit chain, fix. Rank worst-first. End with: (a) the launch-blocker list, and (b) a short "defense-in-depth we should add" list (e.g. cgroups, AppArmor, noexec /tmp, inode quotas). Be maximally skeptical — assume the tenant is a skilled attacker who has read all this code.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	#
3	# Prepare a Debian/Ubuntu box to be a Nxeon SHARED-HOSTING node, so the worker
4	# provisioner (worker/hosting.ts) can create isolated customer accounts on it.
5	# Idempotent — safe to re-run. Run as root ON THE SHARED BOX (not the panel).
6	#
7	#   bash onboard-hosting-node.sh
8	#
9	# What it sets up (the provisioner assumes all of this):
10	#   - nginx + php-fpm (8.3) + mariadb-server
11	#   - an nginx include dir for per-account vhosts (sites-enabled/*)
12	#   - a php-fpm pool include dir (/etc/php/8.3/fpm/pool.d already exists)
13	#   - disk QUOTA enabled on the filesystem holding /home (usrquota)
14	#   - fail2ban (sshd + a basic nginx jail)
15	#   - a default catch-all vhost so an unmatched Host header does NOT leak the
16	#     first account's site (name-based hosting hazard)
17	#
18	# SECURITY: this box will run many customers' PHP side by side. Before selling,
19	# also layer ModSecurity + a malware scanner (ImunifyAV / clamav) and review the
20	# per-account isolation the provisioner applies (open_basedir, disable_functions,
21	# nologin shell, socket perms). See worker/hosting.ts.
22	set -euo pipefail
23	
24	log() { printf '\033[1;36m[hosting-node]\033[0m %s\n' "$*"; }
25	
26	export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
27	PHP_VER="${PHP_VER:-8.3}"
28	
29	log "Installing packages…"
30	apt-get update -y
31	apt-get install -y nginx mariadb-server "php${PHP_VER}-fpm" "php${PHP_VER}-mysql" \
32	  "php${PHP_VER}-cli" "php${PHP_VER}-curl" "php${PHP_VER}-gd" "php${PHP_VER}-mbstring" \
33	  "php${PHP_VER}-xml" "php${PHP_VER}-zip" quota fail2ban certbot python3-certbot-nginx curl >/dev/null
34	
35	log "Ensuring nginx include for per-account vhosts…"
36	mkdir -p /etc/nginx/sites-available /etc/nginx/sites-enabled /var/www/html
37	grep -q 'include /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf || \
38	  sed -i '/http {/a \    include /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*.conf;' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
39	
40	log "Installing a default catch-all vhost (so an unmatched Host never leaks an account)…"
41	cat > /etc/nginx/sites-available/000-default-catchall.conf <<'EOF'
42	# Name-based hosting: a request whose Host matches no account must NOT fall
43	# through to whichever vhost nginx loaded first. This default_server absorbs them.
44	server {
45	    listen 80 default_server;
46	    listen [::]:80 default_server;
47	    server_name _;
48	    root /var/www/html;
49	    location ^~ /.well-known/acme-challenge/ { root /var/www/html; }
50	    location / { return 404; }
51	}
52	EOF
53	ln -sfn /etc/nginx/sites-available/000-default-catchall.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/000-default-catchall.conf
54	rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default 2>/dev/null || true
55	
56	log "Setting up ENFORCED disk quota for tenant homes…"
57	# Two gotchas make naive quota setup silently no-op on a stock Ubuntu cloud image
58	# (learned the hard way validating hosting-1, 2026-08-01):
59	#   1. The qfmt_v2 kernel module ships in linux-modules-extra, which the minimal
60	#      image omits — so ext4_enable_quotas fails with ESRCH and NOTHING enforces.
61	#   2. Enabling the ext4 quota FEATURE on the already-mounted root fs cannot be
62	#      done live, and doing it offline still leaves the quota inodes uninitialised.
63	# The reliable fix: install the modules, and back tenant homes with a DEDICATED
64	# loopback ext4 created WITH the quota feature (mkfs -O quota initialises the
65	# quota inodes properly). Idempotent.
66	DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y "linux-modules-extra-$(uname -r)" quota >/dev/null 2>&1 \
67	  || log "  WARNING: linux-modules-extra install failed — quota may not enforce"
68	depmod -a 2>/dev/null || true
69	modprobe qfmt_v2 2>/dev/null || true
70	
71	HOME_IMG=/var/lib/hosting-home.img
72	if ! mountpoint -q /home || ! quotaon -p /home 2>/dev/null | grep -qi ' is on'; then
73	  if [ ! -f "$HOME_IMG" ]; then
74	    FREE_G=$(df -BG --output=avail / | tail -1 | tr -dc '0-9'); [ -z "$FREE_G" ] && FREE_G=20
75	    SZ=$(( FREE_G * 8 / 10 )); [ "$SZ" -lt 10 ] && SZ=10
76	    log "  creating ${SZ}G quota-enabled home filesystem…"
77	    fallocate -l "${SZ}G" "$HOME_IMG" 2>/dev/null || dd if=/dev/zero of="$HOME_IMG" bs=1M count=$((SZ*1024)) status=none
78	    mkfs.ext4 -q -F -O quota "$HOME_IMG"
79	  fi
80	  # Migrate any existing /home content in, then mount the loopback over /home.
81	  TMP=/var/lib/hosting-home.mnt; mkdir -p "$TMP"
82	  mount -o loop,usrquota,grpquota "$HOME_IMG" "$TMP" && { cp -a /home/. "$TMP/" 2>/dev/null || true; umount "$TMP"; }
83	  mount -o loop,usrquota,grpquota "$HOME_IMG" /home
84	fi
85	# Persist the mount via a systemd unit, NOT fstab: a loop+quota mount in fstab
86	# runs too early (before the loop device / quota module are ready) and silently
87	# fails, dropping quota on every reboot. This oneshot runs after local-fs and
88	# before the web services, and was verified to survive reboots on hosting-1.
89	cat > /etc/systemd/system/nxeon-hosting-home.service <<UNIT
90	[Unit]
91	Description=Nxeon shared-hosting tenant-home quota mount
92	After=local-fs.target
93	Before=nginx.service php${PHP_VER}-fpm.service mariadb.service
94	ConditionPathExists=$HOME_IMG
95	
96	[Service]
97	Type=oneshot
98	RemainAfterExit=yes
99	ExecStart=/bin/sh -c "mountpoint -q /home || mount -o loop,usrquota,grpquota $HOME_IMG /home"
100	ExecStart=/bin/sh -c "modprobe qfmt_v2 2>/dev/null || true; quotaon /home 2>/dev/null || true"
101	
102	[Install]
103	WantedBy=multi-user.target
104	UNIT
105	# Make sure any stale fstab loop line from an earlier version can't fight the unit.
106	sed -i "\#$HOME_IMG#d" /etc/fstab 2>/dev/null || true
107	systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl enable --now nxeon-hosting-home.service >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
108	quotaon /home 2>/dev/null || true
109	if quotaon -p /home 2>/dev/null | grep -qi ' is on'; then

I'm examining the Prisma schema to understand the hosting models, and I notice a potential SQL injection vulnerability in the WordPress installation command where the database password is wrapped in single quotes without proper escaping.

Looking at the validation logic, I see that dbPass is only checked for truthiness rather than character validation, but it turns out the password is server-generated as alphanumeric base64url output, so it's safe. The adminPass is properly validated with a strict regex pattern, and adminEmail uses SAFE_EMAIL validation. Since the payload is always created server-side and the tenant can only trigger the installation action, the injection risk is mitigated.

For app installations, the recipe URL comes from a hardcoded map and the slug is validated against it, so that's secure. But the cron command validation is the real concern — it allows nearly any characters except newlines and carriage returns, up to 500 characters. The dangerous part is that cron jobs run outside the PHP-FPM pool, so PHP's disable_functions and open_basedir restrictions don't apply. A tenant could inject arbitrary shell commands into a cron job that executes as the jailed unix user with a real shell.

The unix user is only confined via SFTP chroot, which only applies to SSH sessions through sshd. Cron doesn't use sshd, so cron jobs run as the unix user in the actual filesystem without chroot restrictions. This means the entire PHP sandbox can be bypassed through a malicious cron job that gives the tenant full filesystem read access as their unix user.

Looking at what they could actually access: other tenants' home directories are protected by unix permissions (711 root:root), and their webroots are 2750 with different owners, so cross-tenant file reads are blocked. But system files like /etc/nginx are world-readable, and /etc/letsencrypt with private keys is typically root-owned 700, which they can't access either.

The real problem is that cron shell access lets them run arbitrary code as their unix user completely outside the PHP sandbox — compilers, network tools, kernel exploits, anything world-readable, resource exhaustion attacks. They could try reading /etc/ssl/hosting/<user> (700 root, so blocked), but the fundamental issue is that cron bypasses all the hardening. Without cron, they'd be stuck with just PHP execution and chrooted SFTP, both heavily restricted. Cron jobs bypass the disable_functions restrictions entirely since they run under the CLI php.ini rather than the FPM pool configuration, making this a complete hardening bypass. The resource limits on the FPM pool (6 children, 256MB memory each) provide some containment per tenant, but that's still substantial capacity for abuse.

The real vulnerability is the complete absence of CPU limits, cgroup restrictions, or process ID caps. A single tenant could launch a fork bomb via cron that exhausts PIDs system-wide and crashes the entire box, affecting all other tenants. There's no ulimit configuration, no nproc limits in /etc/security/limits.conf, and no systemd cgroup isolation. Disk quotas exist, but that's the only meaningful resource boundary.

The inode limit is also completely open—the setquota command sets both soft and hard inode limits to 0, meaning unlimited. A malicious tenant could create millions of tiny files to exhaust inodes on the shared /home filesystem, causing a denial of service for everyone. The usage tracking measures inode consumption but has no enforcement mechanism.

For open_basedir, the configuration restricts PHP to the user's home directory and /usr/share/php, which is reasonable.

However, there's a critical prefix-matching vulnerability: open_basedir does prefix matching without requiring a trailing slash, so `/home/nxfoo` would also match `/home/nxfoobar/...` and allow access to other users' directories. This is a known PHP gotcha where the restriction is treated as a path prefix rather than a directory boundary.

The real question is whether an attacker could engineer a username collision—getting their username to be a prefix of a victim's. Since usernames are derived as `nx` + 8 alphanumeric characters from the email + 6 random hex characters, and then sliced to 16 characters, it's theoretically possible but difficult to control precisely. The attacker would need to craft their email localpart and hope the random suffix aligns in a way that creates a prefix match with a victim's username.

But there's a more direct vulnerability here: the `open_basedir` configuration lacks a trailing slash, so `/home/nxATTACKER` would match paths like `/home/nxATTACKERxyz` due to prefix matching. This is a real high-severity finding—cross-tenant file read via incomplete path matching. The fix is straightforward: append a trailing slash to make it `/home/nxATTACKER/`, which prevents the prefix collision. The `chdir` and `upload_tmp_dir` settings are already properly scoped under the home directory, so those are fine.

For the self-signed certificate generation, the domain is validated through a strict regex check before being passed to the OpenSSL command, so there's no injection risk even though it runs as root.

The SSH connection as root with an encrypted password is the next thing to examine.

For the vhost installation using a heredoc, the configuration is built from validated domain, username, and paths—the domain regex prevents newlines so there's no way to break out of the heredoc delimiter. The delimiter itself is quoted, preventing any variable expansion.

Now I'm looking at the cross-tenant database scope issue.  The database user is derived from the tenant's username and slug, so since each username is unique per node, another tenant can't create a colliding user. The termination logic properly scopes database drops using the username prefix pattern. Moving on to MySQL grants.

The FILE privilege isn't included in database-scoped GRANT ALL since it's a global privilege, and `secure_file_priv` isn't granted anyway, so that's secure. For the restore process, backups are extracted to a root-only staging area then copied back to the tenant's home directory. The SQL dumps are replayed as root, which is fine since they're root-generated.

The tar archive itself combines the tenant's home directory with the root-owned database dumps, but since the tar is created by root and stored in a 700-permission directory owned by root, tenants can't tamper with it — the dumps remain trustworthy. Now I'm checking whether the parent directory `/var/hosting-backups` itself is properly protected.

The per-user subdirectories are set to 700 root, so tenants running via cron can't read their own backup directory. That's secure. But when restoring, the mysql command runs as root with the dump filename, and I need to verify whether mysqldump includes `USE` or `CREATE DATABASE` statements — if not, the restore might fail or behave unexpectedly.

The database namespace query uses `SHOW DATABASES LIKE '${u}\\_%'`, and since usernames are validated alphanumeric, there's no injection risk there. Health and usage sweeps run as root with curl and find, but the directory and user variables are validated, so that's fine. The authorization checks look solid — every action verifies `userId` matches or the user is admin — though I'm noticing the `revealHostingSftpPassword` endpoint needs careful review since it exposes credentials to owners or admins.

Actually, there's a gap: `revealHostingSftpPassword` doesn't call `assertNotImpersonating`, unlike other sensitive actions. An impersonating admin could leak a customer's SFTP password. Same issue with `listHostingTasks`, which returns one-time WordPress admin passwords — an impersonating admin could read those. These are the customer's own credentials, so impersonation is a concern here. The file manager connects as a jailed SFTP user with chroot restrictions, which is the right approach.

But I'm noticing a potential DoS vector: `fsWriteBuffer` and `fsReadBuffer` have no size limits. A tenant could request reading a massive file, causing the Node panel process to buffer the entire thing in memory and crash — that's a platform-wide DoS affecting all tenants, not just the requester. They already have SFTP access anyway, so this is a medium-severity issue on the panel side.

I also see `hostingListFiles`, `hostingMkdir`, and `hostingDeleteFile` exposed, but I don't see where the upload/download actions are defined — they might be elsewhere. Worth tracking down.

On the mount configuration side, the home loopback is set up with quotas but lacks `noexec`, `nosuid`, and `nodev` flags. That means a tenant could place and execute binaries from their home directory via cron, which is a minor risk since they can't create SUID files they don't own anyway, but `noexec` would add defense in depth here.

The onboarding script relies heavily on best-effort security measures — ModSecurity, ClamAV, fail2ban, and quotas all have fallback logging rather than hard enforcement. The fail2ban nginx jail for HTTP auth doesn't really apply here, and there's no real per-tenant isolation layer. These are staged protections with gaps.

I'm also checking the completeness of `PHP_DISABLED_FUNCTIONS` — it covers the obvious ones like `exec`, `passthru`, `shell_exec`, `system`, `proc_open`, `popen`, and the `pcntl_*` functions.  But there's a critical gap: `mb_send_mail` isn't disabled, so a tenant can bypass the `mail` function block by using that alternative. Functions like `proc_get_status`, `proc_terminate`, and `proc_close` are less critical since `proc_open` is already blocked, and `imap_open` has historical RCE risks but requires the imap extension.

The real issue is that `disable_functions` can be circumvented through cron shell access anyway, but within PHP itself the `mb_send_mail` bypass creates a spam vector. Language constructs like `include` and `eval` can't be disabled, and `assert` or `create_function` aren't concerns on PHP 8.x.

The upload directory and session paths are properly contained within `open_basedir`, so that's secure.

`putenv` is disabled in PHP which blocks the LD_PRELOAD trick, though cron shell could set environment variables freely. For symlinks, the chroot jail neutralizes them since symlinks resolve within the chroot boundary, and PHP has symlink disabled anyway — though the cron shell could still create them.

But here's the real issue: nginx doesn't have `disable_symlinks` configured, so if a tenant creates a symlink in their webroot via cron (in the real filesystem, not the chroot) pointing to something like /etc/passwd, nginx running as www-data would follow it and serve that file if www-data can read it. That's a direct path to leaking world-readable files.

Even worse, since every webroot is owned by its tenant but has www-data as the group with read-execute permissions (2750), and nginx runs as www-data, a tenant could symlink to another tenant's wp-config.php or other sensitive files in their webroot. nginx would happily follow that symlink and serve the victim's config file to the attacker—a critical cross-tenant information disclosure. The attacker can browse to the symlink through nginx, which resolves it outside the chroot context and reads the victim's file. Even via chrooted SFTP, an absolute symlink with a target pointing outside the chroot would work because nginx operates on the real filesystem, not within the chroot—so the question becomes whether SFTP allows creating symlinks with absolute paths that escape the chroot boundary. So the attacker bypasses the need for cron entirely—a single SFTP symlink combined with an HTTP request lets them read any file accessible to www-data across all tenants, including wp-config.php with database credentials. This is a critical vulnerability. The architecture itself—with 2750 permissions and www-data as a shared group reader—creates a confused deputy scenario where nginx resolves symlinks against the real filesystem rather than the chroot boundary. Mitigations like `disable_symlinks on;` in nginx, restricting www-data's group access, or per-tenant workers would prevent this, but none are implemented. Hardlinks present the same vulnerability since they bypass the webroot restriction entirely—nginx reads them just as it would symlinks. The fundamental issue is that a shared nginx instance with www-data as a universal group reader creates a confused-deputy problem where one tenant can access another's files. Proper mitigations include using `disable_symlinks if_not_owner;` in nginx config, separating static file serving per tenant, or implementing per-tenant groups and nginx processes—though cPanel's mod_ruid2 approach shows one way to solve this at scale. yle if_not_owner stops symlink traversal, but hardlinks bypass this since they point to the same inode without owner distinction. However, the `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` sysctl (enabled by default on modern kernels) prevents unprivileged users from creating hardlinks to files they don't own, so hardlink attacks are likely already blocked — but symlink attacks remain fully exploitable without the disable_symlinks directive.

Now I need to verify the Prisma schema for other vulnerabilities and check the nginx PHP location block. The current fastcgi configuration passes `$document_root$fastcgi_script_name` directly to SCRIPT_FILENAME without validating the file exists or using `try_files`, which combined with `cgi.fix_pathinfo=1` could allow path traversal and arbitrary PHP execution.…

The upload path combines a query parameter with a sanitized filename, and while the directory comes directly from user input, the safeRel function rejects path traversal attempts like `..`, so `path=../../etc` would be blocked. The filename itself gets stripped of problematic characters, and everything operates within a chrooted SFTP environment anyway. Now I'm thinking through the download path security.

The download reads the entire file into memory without any size limit, which could let a tenant cause memory exhaustion on the shared panel process if they upload a massive file via SFTP and then download it through this route — that's a low-priority DoS concern since it's their own file. I should verify the cron setup: the onboard script doesn't configure login.defs or resource limits for the tenant user, and PHP CLI is installed, so cron jobs can run arbitrary shell commands as the unix user, bypassing any FPM disable_functions restrictions. The SFTP chroot with ForceCommand internal-sftp prevents shell access, so the only unsandboxed code execution paths for a tenant are cron jobs and potentially a symlink trick.

Cron actually does run even though the user's login shell is /usr/sbin/nologin, because cron uses /bin/sh by default rather than respecting the passwd shell entry. Locking the password with usermod -L doesn't stop cron either. So cron is effectively a jail escape — it's arbitrary shell execution as an unprivileged user, which completely defeats the PHP sandbox (open_basedir, disable_functions) that the platform markets as the isolation boundary. From a shell, a tenant can trivially perform cross-tenant symlink reads, fork bombs, or attempt kernel privilege escalation exploits.

I'm rating cron as HIGH severity since it enables the sandbox bypass and serves as the launch pad for further attacks, while the symlink cross-tenant read is CRITICAL because it works independently and directly steals wp-config.php. The underlying bug is real and trivial to fix with a trailing slash, so I'm marking it MEDIUM severity for correctness rather than HIGH, though I'll note the prefix mechanism as a contributing factor.

I now have a complete picture. Let me compile the findings.

## Nxeon Shared-Hosting — Adversarial Security Audit

Threat model applied: a malicious paying tenant with a PHP-FPM pool + panel-driven cron + chrooted SFTP, on a live multi-tenant box (`ENABLE_SHARED_HOSTING=1`). Read-only review of branch `feature/shared-hosting-p0` in `/opt/nxeon-wt-host`. Nothing was modified or executed.

The code is genuinely careful about the things it set out to defend (shell-injection, GRANT wildcard bleed, TOCTOU on caps, IDOR, backup SQL tampering — those are all solid). The gaps are structural: the isolation model has a confused-deputy read primitive and an unsandboxed code-exec primitive that together defeat the PHP jail, plus no resource containment at all.

---

### CRITICAL-1 — Cross-tenant file read via symlink + the shared `www-data`-readable webroot (steals every tenant's `wp-config.php`)
**Files:** `lib/hosting.ts:238-243` (`accountFsPlan`: webroot `2750 <user>:www-data`), `worker/hosting.ts:115-152` / `167-204` (vhosts have no `disable_symlinks`), plus the chrooted SFTP that still lets a tenant create absolute symlinks.

Every tenant's webroot is mode `2750 <user>:www-data`, and the single nginx runs as `www-data` — so **nginx can read every tenant's files by group**. The only thing normally stopping cross-tenant reads is that each vhost `root` points at that tenant's own dir. A symlink defeats that:

Exploit chain (no cron needed, pure SFTP + a browser):
1. Attacker connects via their chrooted SFTP and creates `public_html/steal` → a symlink whose literal target string is `/home/nxvictim/public_html/wp-config.php`. Inside the chroot the link looks broken; the target string is stored verbatim.
2. Attacker browses `https://attacker-domain/steal`. nginx (not chrooted, running as `www-data`) resolves the absolute target against the real filesystem, and `www-data` is the group owner of the victim's webroot (`2750`), so it **reads and serves the victim's `wp-config.php`** — DB name, DB user, DB password, auth salts.
3. MariaDB binds localhost and tenant grants are `@'localhost'`, but the attacker now has the victim's DB creds and can reach them from their own PHP/cron on the same box → full read/write of the victim's database.

`location ~ /\. { deny all; }` only blocks dotfiles; a link named `steal` is served statically, bypassing FPM/`open_basedir` entirely (nginx reads it directly). This is the single worst finding and it works against the default WordPress install this platform one-click-provisions.

**Fix:** Add `disable_symlinks if_not_owner;` to every `server`/`location` block that serves tenant content (victim files are owned by the victim, not the attacker, so nginx refuses to follow). Longer term, stop making `www-data` a universal group-reader of all webroots (per-tenant static serving / suexec-style model). Confirm `fs.protected_symlinks=1` and `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` are set on the node (protected_hardlinks blocks the equivalent hardlink variant; it's kernel-default but should be asserted in `onboard-hosting-node.sh`).

---

### HIGH-1 — Panel cron gives unsandboxed shell as the unix user → total bypass of the PHP jail + LPE launch pad
**Files:** `lib/hosting.ts:165-169` (`isValidCronCommand` allows *any* char except `\n\r%`), `worker/hosting.ts:944-956` (`writeUserCrontab`), `lib/actions-hosting.ts:625-646` (`createCron`).

The cron command is deliberately arbitrary and runs via `crontab -u <user>`. The PHP isolation boundary the code repeatedly calls "THE" boundary — `disable_functions`, `open_basedir` — lives **only in the FPM pool**. Cron does not go through PHP-FPM: it runs `/bin/sh` (cron ignores the `nologin` login shell), so:
- `* * * * * php -r 'system("id"); readfile("/home/nxvictim/public_html/wp-config.php");'` runs the **CLI** php.ini (no `disable_functions`, no `open_basedir`), so `system()`/`exec()` are fully live and there is no basedir. Complete jail bypass.
- From that shell the CRITICAL-1 symlink read is trivial, and every local-privilege-escalation avenue (kernel LPE, SUID hunting, writable-service hunting) becomes reachable. Without cron a tenant only has sandboxed PHP + chrooted no-shell SFTP; cron is the one hole that converts that into a normal login shell.

This is arguably "expected" for some shared hosts, but here it silently nullifies the advertised isolation and, combined with HIGH-2 (no resource caps), is a launch blocker.

**Fix:** At minimum run tenant cron under the same restrictions (e.g. a wrapper that execs `php -c <pool-hardened.ini>` only, or systemd-run with the tenant's cgroup slice + `disable_functions` in the CLI ini). Set `disable_functions`/`open_basedir` in the **CLI** php.ini on the node too. If a real shell is intended, treat the box as "tenant has shell" and harden accordingly (cgroups, nosuid/nodev mounts, LPE patching) — don't rely on the FPM pool as the boundary.

---

### HIGH-2 — No CPU / memory / PID / inode containment: one tenant DoSes the whole node
**Files:** `scripts/onboard-hosting-node.sh` (no `limits.conf`, no cgroup/systemd slice, no `TasksMax`), `lib/hosting.ts:260-280` (`fpmPoolConfig` caps only `memory_limit`/`request_terminate_timeout`), `worker/hosting.ts:271` (`setquota … 0 0` = **unlimited inodes**).

Confirmed: **no** per-tenant CPU, RAM, or process/PID cap exists anywhere.
- Via the HIGH-1 cron shell, a classic fork bomb `:(){ :|:& };:` exhausts PIDs/CPU host-wide → every tenant down. No `nproc` limit in `/etc/security/limits.conf`, no `TasksMax`.
- `setquota -u ${u} ${softBlocks} ${hardBlocks} 0 0 /home` sets inode limits to `0 0` = unlimited. A tenant can create millions of empty files and exhaust inodes on the shared `/home` loopback fs, DoSing all tenants — even though `hostingUsageSweep` *measures* `inodesUsed`, nothing caps it.
- FPM caps `pm.max_children = 6` and 256M/child, so PHP alone is roughly bounded; cron is not bounded at all.

**Fix:** Set inode quota (non-zero soft/hard) in the `setquota` call. Add `nproc`/`nofile` caps in `/etc/security/limits.conf` (or per-user systemd slice with `TasksMax=`, `CPUQuota=`, `MemoryMax=`). Put tenant cron/php under a per-tenant cgroup slice. Mount `/home` `nosuid,nodev`.

---

### MEDIUM-1 — `open_basedir` has no trailing slash → prefix-match escape between tenants
**File:** `lib/hosting.ts:273` — `php_admin_value[open_basedir] = ${home}:/usr/share/php`.

PHP treats `open_basedir` entries without a trailing slash as **path prefixes**, not directories. `open_basedir = /home/nxbob` also authorizes `/home/nxbob2xyz/...`. If two same-node usernames are in a prefix relationship (usernames are `nx`+base+random, capped at 16 chars — coincidental but grindable by registering many accounts), tenant `nxbob` reads `nxbobxyz`'s files straight from PHP with no symlink needed.

**Fix:** `${home}/:/usr/share/php/` (trailing slashes on every component).

---

### MEDIUM-2 — `mail` blocked but `mb_send_mail` is not → PHP spam vector
**File:** `lib/hosting.ts:192-205` (`PHP_DISABLED_FUNCTIONS`).

`mail` is disabled, but `mb_send_mail()` (mbstring is installed per `onboard-hosting-node.sh:32`) is an equivalent wrapper and is **not** in the list, so a tenant's PHP can still send mail and turn the shared IP into a spam source (reputation damage for every tenant on the IP). Also consider `imap_open` (RCE-historically) if `php-imap` ever gets added.

**Fix:** Add `mb_send_mail` (and `mail` stays). Prefer a sendmail wrapper that rate-limits/authenticates instead of a blocklist.

---

### MEDIUM-3 — Panel file download buffers whole file into the shared Node process (memory DoS)
**Files:** `lib/hosting-fs.ts:91-100` (`fsReadBuffer` → `Buffer.concat` of the entire file), `app/api/hosting/files/route.ts:40-53` (GET has no size cap; upload has `MAX_UPLOAD` but download does not).

A tenant SFTPs a multi-GB file into their own home, then requests it through the download route. The panel/worker process buffers the whole file in memory → OOM of the **shared platform process**, affecting all customers and the admin panel. (The path itself is safe — `safeRel` + chroot.)

**Fix:** Stream the response (pipe the SFTP read stream to the HTTP response) and enforce a max download size.

---

### LOW-1 — `revealHostingSftpPassword` missing `assertNotImpersonating`
**File:** `lib/actions-hosting.ts:190-198`.

Every other sensitive action (`orderHostingAccount`, `createHostingDatabase`, `ownedSiteAccount`) calls `assertNotImpersonating()`. This one does not, so an admin impersonating a customer can reveal that customer's plaintext SFTP/unix password. `listHostingTasks` (`actions-hosting.ts:309`) similarly surfaces one-time WordPress admin passwords to an impersonating admin.

**Fix:** Add `await assertNotImpersonating()` to `revealHostingSftpPassword` (and consider it for the task-result reveal).

---

### Things I checked that are SOLID (so the launch list stays focused)
- **Shell injection:** every interpolated username/domain/php-version/cron-field is validated against strict allowlists before hitting a shell; heredocs are quoted (`<<'VH'`, `<<'NXCRONEOF'`), so no breakout. WordPress/app installs use server-generated (not tenant-supplied) alphanumeric creds. No injection found in provisioner, backup, restore, lifecycle, or SSL paths.
- **MySQL isolation:** `buildScopedGrantSql` escapes `_`/`%` (no wildcard bleed), grants are db-scoped (no global FILE/SUPER), users are `<user>_*`-namespaced, MariaDB binds localhost with anon users/`test` dropped.
- **Backup/restore cross-tenant:** DB dumps are root-owned outside the tenant tree and only `${u}_*.sql` are replayed (the previously-noted tenant-tamper vuln is genuinely fixed); the stored tar sits in `700 root` dirs.
- **IDOR/authz:** all read/write actions enforce `userId === user.id || ADMIN`; hostname uniqueness is checked across all three tables (`isHostnameClaimed`); caps enforced in `Serializable` transactions closing the TOCTOU.
- **SFTP jail:** file manager connects **as the tenant** through the OS chroot (not root), so a planted symlink can't escape *the SFTP session* (it escapes only via nginx — CRITICAL-1); `safeRel` is defense-in-depth.
- **sshd change** is `sshd -t`-guarded before reload (can't lock the box out).

---

### (a) Launch-blocker list (fix before paid ad traffic)
1. **CRITICAL-1** — cross-tenant read via symlink; add `disable_symlinks if_not_owner;` to all tenant vhosts (and confirm `fs.protected_symlinks/hardlinks=1`). This is exploitable *today* against the default WordPress install.
2. **HIGH-1** — cron = unsandboxed shell that voids the PHP jail; either sandbox cron or accept "tenant has shell" and harden the node for LPE. Also set `disable_functions`/`open_basedir` in the CLI php.ini.
3. **HIGH-2** — add PID/CPU/inode caps (non-zero inode quota, `nproc` limit / systemd slice). Without these, one $3.29 tenant can take the node down.
4. **MEDIUM-1** — trailing-slash `open_basedir` (one-line fix, ship it with the batch).
5. **MEDIUM-2** — add `mb_send_mail` to the blocklist (IP-reputation protection before ads point at the box).

### (b) Defense-in-depth to add
- **nginx:** `disable_symlinks if_not_owner`, `autoindex off` (confirm), a global `server` that rejects unknown SNI on 443 (the catch-all is HTTP-only today — an unmatched HTTPS Host falls through to whichever 443 block loaded first).
- **Mounts:** `/home` loopback mounted `nosuid,nodev` (currently only `usrquota,grpquota`); consider `noexec` on `/home/*/tmp` (blocks dropped-binary execution via the cron shell).
- **cgroups / systemd slices** per tenant (`CPUQuota`, `MemoryMax`, `TasksMax`) — the real containment layer that's entirely absent.
- **Inode quota** (fix the `0 0`) and a global reserve so quota exhaustion can't wedge the fs.
- **AppArmor/seccomp** profile for the tenant FPM pools and cron wrapper.
- **CLI php.ini hardening** mirroring the FPM pool (`disable_functions`, `open_basedir`) so `php` from cron isn't a free sandbox bypass.
- **Sendmail policy:** replace the `mail`/`mb_send_mail` blocklist with an authenticated, rate-limited relay.
- **Harden the node's main sshd** for tenant users at the global level (`AllowTcpForwarding no`, `PermitTunnel no`) so it doesn't depend solely on the per-user `Match` block.
- The onboarding hardening (ModSecurity/ClamAV/quota) is **best-effort with `|| log warning`** — several steps silently no-op on a minimal image. Add a hard pre-sell verification gate that refuses to mark a node `ONLINE` unless quota is enforcing, ModSecurity loaded, and the malware scan cron present.

Key files: `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/lib/hosting.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/worker/hosting.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/lib/actions-hosting.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/lib/hosting-fs.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/app/api/hosting/files/route.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/scripts/onboard-hosting-node.sh`, `/opt/nxeon-wt-host/prisma/schema.prisma`.
